1. Core Clinical Tension: A middle-aged man presents with a 9-month history of painless, cystic muscular swellings and masses across both lower extremities without systemic B-symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats), mimicking soft tissue neoplasms, rhabdomyolysis, or inflammatory myopathy, following a course of corticosteroid immunosuppression.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint is reached after clinical evaluation, normal baseline serum muscle enzymes, inflammatory markers, ultrasound, and lower-extremity MRI, immediately prior to deep invasive muscle biopsy, interferon-gamma release assay, and mycobacterial PCR/cultures.
3. Differential Distinctions: Rhabdomyolysis is ruled out by completely normal serum creatine kinase and aldolase levels and a chronic 9-month indolent course. Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy or neuromuscular disease is disproven by normal motor conduction and absence of spontaneous denervation on electromyography. The critical history of prior pulmonary infection and 6 months of steroid immunosuppression raises suspicion for latent mycobacterial reactivation in an atypical extraskeletal site.
case_prompt:
A 49-year-old male presented with a 9-month history of multifocal lower-extremity pain, localized swelling, and palpable masses in the bilateral thighs and calves. The swellings had gradually increased in size and number over several months. One month prior to admission, he developed similar but milder symptoms in the left forearm without discrete masses. He reported no fever, chills, night sweats, malaise, anorexia, weight loss, or local trauma. His medical history was notable for a prior treated pulmonary infection and non-infectious posterior uveitis treated with systemic corticosteroids for 6 months one year prior.

On physical examination, vital signs were normal. Musculoskeletal examination revealed multiple well-demarcated, cystic-feeling masses in the bilateral thighs and calves. The masses were non-fluctuant, non-tender, and without local warmth or erythema. Neurological examination was intact.

Laboratory testing demonstrated a normal complete blood count, normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, normal C-reactive protein, and normal rheumatoid factor. Serum muscle enzymes and metabolic markers, including creatine kinase (CK), aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase, AST, and ALT, were all within normal reference ranges. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) were low-titer positive at 1:100, fungal G-test was negative, and blood parasite screens were negative. Musculoskeletal ultrasound revealed solid-appearing substantive lesions within the calf musculature bilaterally. Chest computed tomography showed changes consistent with prior resolved pulmonary infection. Musculoskeletal MRI of the lower extremities demonstrated diffuse abnormal signal intensity involving bilateral calf and thigh musculature, interpreted as concerning for an infectious process or myopathy.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: An outside MRI initially suggested rhabdomyolysis due to a history of strenuous exercise. However, serum creatine kinase, aldolase, and transaminases were completely normal, and an indolent 9-month progression of discrete muscular masses is inconsistent with acute rhabdomyolysis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient underwent a musculoskeletal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) examination in a local hospital; the results were reported as suggestive for rhabdomyolysis, only according to his history of strenuous exercise... Further examinations, including those for hemogram, rheumatoid factor (RF), C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), creatine kinase (CK), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), fungal G-test, and tumor marker levels, were within normal limits.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Diffuse abnormal muscular signals on MRI can represent inflammatory myopathy. However, muscle enzymes were normal, electromyography showed normal sensory and motor nerve conduction without irritable myopathic motor units, and the patient had localized pseudo-tumoral masses rather than symmetric proximal weakness.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Musculoskeletal MRI (Figure 2) examination showed diffuse abnormal signals on the bilateral calf and thigh muscles, suggesting infectious lesions or myopathy. Electromyography (EMG) examination showed that sensory and motor conduction are normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Deep surgical biopsy of the gastrocnemius muscle demonstrated granulomatous inflammation with Langhans giant cells and epithelioid histiocytes. While acid-fast staining and tuberculin skin testing were negative, tissue PCR and culture of the calf muscle mass confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A deep biopsy (including skin, subcutis, fascia, and muscle) was performed on the right gastrocnemius (including the mass and nearby muscles), and the results showed lymphocytes and plasma cell infiltration into and around non-necrotic muscle fibers without muscle fiber necrosis and regeneration. Moreover, inflammation granulomas (including Langerhans cells, epithelioid cells, and lymphocytes) were visible under the microscope... PCR for the M. tuberculosis complex presented positivity, and a tuberculosis T-SPOT test(+); M. tuberculosis was found in biopsy tissue culture of the mass on the calf.

editor_comments: Standardized admission diagnostic case for muscular tuberculosis. The admission breakpoint cleanly captures clinical presentation and imaging prior to deep muscle biopsy, T-SPOT, and mycobacterial PCR/culture.
